title: Population Genetics
tagline: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, selection, drift, mutation and migration, inbreeding, linkage disequilibrium, molecular evolution and quantitative traits
summary: Population genetics turns Mendel’s laws into a quantitative theory of evolution. This course builds the classical models — Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, selection, genetic drift, mutation, migration and inbreeding — then connects them to DNA sequence data through linkage disequilibrium and the neutral theory, and to continuous traits through heritability and the response to selection.

chapters.title: Genetic variation and Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
chapters.summary: Measuring variation, allele and genotype frequencies, and the null model of a population that is not evolving.

chapters.title: Natural selection in populations
chapters.summary: Fitness, selection coefficients, dominance and the dynamics of allele frequencies under selection.

chapters.title: Genetic drift and effective population size
chapters.summary: The Wright–Fisher model, fixation probabilities, coalescence and the effective population size.

chapters.title: Mutation, migration and population structure
chapters.summary: Mutation–selection balance, gene flow, the island model and F-statistics.

chapters.title: Inbreeding and non-random mating
chapters.summary: The inbreeding coefficient, assortative mating and inbreeding depression.

chapters.title: Linkage disequilibrium
chapters.summary: Associations between loci, how recombination breaks them down, and what they reveal about population history.

chapters.title: Molecular evolution and the neutral theory
chapters.summary: The molecular clock, rates of substitution and tests for selection in DNA sequences.

chapters.title: Quantitative traits
chapters.summary: Polygenic inheritance, genetic and environmental variance, and heritability.

chapters.title: The response to selection
chapters.summary: The breeder’s equation, artificial selection and correlated responses.
